uzbek: Rostdan ham ... haqida o'ylab ko'rishingiz kerak.
usage: Used when gently nudging someone towards an idea without sounding too pushy or demanding.
grammar_pattern: You should really consider + V-ing/noun
example_sentences: You should really consider studying abroad to improve your English.
You should really consider taking the bus; it's much cheaper than a taxi.
If you want to pass the exam, you should really consider attending the extra classes.
You should really consider buying this laptop while it is on sale.
You should really consider moving to a quieter area for your health.
native_notes: Adding 'really' makes the advice feel more sincere and less like a command.

usage: Used to draw attention to a key fact that supports your argument during a debate or essay.
grammar_pattern: It's worth noting that + clause
common_mistakes: It is worth to note that
alternatives: It is important to mention that
We must keep in mind that
It is relevant to point out that
example_sentences: It’s worth noting that renewable energy is becoming more affordable every year.
It’s worth noting that the majority of students prefer online learning.
While the plan is ambitious, it’s worth noting that the budget is quite limited.
It’s worth noting that early registration saves you twenty percent.
It’s worth noting that healthy eating habits can prevent long-term illness.
native_notes: Used when you want to subtly steer someone toward your viewpoint by introducing an undeniable fact.

expression: Don't you think it’s better to...?
usage: A rhetorical question used to persuade someone by suggesting a better alternative while sounding polite.
grammar_pattern: Don't you think + it's better to + verb?
common_mistakes: Do you not think is it better
Don't you think it better to
alternatives: Don't you agree that it is better to...?
example_sentences: Don't you think it’s better to finish the project today than to rush tomorrow?
Don't you think it’s better to travel by train to see the landscape?
Don't you think it’s better to discuss these issues face-to-face?
Don't you think it’s better to save money for an emergency?
Don't you think it’s better to be honest about your mistakes?
synonyms: Isn't it a better idea to
native_notes: The negative structure ('Don't you...') invites agreement and makes your suggestion feel like a shared conclusion.
russian: ... тебе не кажется, что так лучше сделать?

uzbek: Siz uchun ... qilgan yaxshiroq bo'lar edi.
usage: Used to give practical, direct advice to someone when you believe their current path is not ideal.
grammar_pattern: You'd (you would) be much better off + V-ing
common_mistakes: You would be much better to
alternatives: It would be in your best interest to...
You would have a better result if you...
example_sentences: You’d be much better off preparing for the exam a month in advance.
You’d be much better off taking the train; the traffic is terrible today.
You’d be much better off focusing on your strengths than worrying about your weaknesses.
You’d be much better off renting a place near your office.
You’d be much better off talking to your boss directly instead of emailing.
synonyms: It would be better for you to
native_notes: Very common in spoken British English. The phrase assumes you have already weighed the situation and are offering a superior outcome.

usage: Used in academic or professional settings to introduce a key factor the listener might have overlooked.
grammar_pattern: It's worth bearing in mind (that) + clause
common_mistakes: It is worth to bear in mind
It is worth of bearing in mind
example_sentences: It's worth bearing in mind that the deadline is strictly tomorrow.
While technology is helpful, it's worth bearing in mind that human interaction is essential.
It's worth bearing in mind that market prices can fluctuate unexpectedly.
Before making a decision, it's worth bearing in mind all the potential risks.
It's worth bearing in mind that study abroad requires significant preparation.
native_notes: A very polite way to introduce a warning or a piece of evidence during a debate or meeting.

usage: Used to direct someone's attention to a piece of evidence that makes your point obvious.
grammar_pattern: Just look at + noun phrase
example_sentences: Just look at how much the city has changed in the last decade.
Just look at the success rate of this method; it clearly works.
Just look at the cost of living nowadays; it's impossible to save.
Just look at these statistics before you decide to quit.
Just look at how happy they are; the decision was clearly correct.
native_notes: Very punchy and direct. Effective in oral arguments, but avoid in formal writing.

usage: Used to pressure someone into agreeing with an undeniable point or fact.
grammar_pattern: You've got to admit (that) + clause
example_sentences: You've got to admit that the new campus facilities are impressive.
You've got to admit, this is a much better solution than the previous one.
You've got to admit that the traffic is much worse during peak hours.
You've got to admit, we would have finished earlier if we had started sooner.
You've got to admit that she has a point about the budget cuts.
native_notes: Slightly assertive; often used in a friendly but firm debate.

usage: Used to challenge the other person's perspective, implying that your point is logically obvious.
grammar_pattern: Surely you can see (that) + clause
example_sentences: Surely you can see why this project is so important for our future.
Surely you can see that his argument is based on outdated data.
Surely you can see that waiting any longer will only make things harder.
Surely you can see the value in investing early.
Surely you can see that the current system is no longer sustainable.
native_notes: Use with caution; it can sound slightly patronizing if said with the wrong tone.

expression: You should really give it a go
usage: Used to encourage someone to try a new experience or activity when they are hesitant.
grammar_pattern: You should really + give + it + a go
common_mistakes: You should give to it a go
alternatives: Why not give it a try?
You might as well try it
example_sentences: You should really give it a go, you might actually enjoy the pottery class.
It looks difficult, but you should really give it a go.
If you're bored this weekend, you should really give it a go and join us.
You should really give it a go before deciding you don't like it.
Honestly, you should really give it a go; what have you got to lose?
native_notes: Very common in casual British English to encourage friends or colleagues to take a risk or step out of their comfort zone.

usage: Used when trying to convince someone who seems to be ignoring the obvious facts.
grammar_pattern: Surely you can see that + clause
example_sentences: Surely you can see that we need a better solution for this project.
Surely you can see that the current plan is unsustainable.
Surely you can see that his argument doesn't hold much weight.
Surely you can see that I'm trying to help you, not criticize you.
Surely you can see that the situation has completely changed since yesterday.
native_notes: Can sound slightly confrontational or condescending if said with the wrong tone, so be careful with your intonation.

expression: Don't you think it would be better to...
usage: A polite, indirect way to steer someone toward your point of view during a discussion.
grammar_pattern: Don't you think it would be better to + verb
common_mistakes: Don't you think it will be better to
Do you not think it is better
alternatives: Might it be better if we...
example_sentences: Don't you think it would be better to address these issues before the deadline?
Don't you think it would be better to talk to him directly?
Don't you think it would be better to stay here until the rain stops?
Don't you think it would be better to save some money for the future?
Don't you think it would be better to get a second opinion?
native_notes: Very useful in IELTS Speaking Part 3 or business meetings where you need to disagree or suggest an alternative without being rude.
russian: Я думаю, не было бы лучше, если бы мы...?

usage: A soft, collaborative way to propose a new idea or persuade a group to change direction.
grammar_pattern: What if we + past tense verb
common_mistakes: What if we will try to
example_sentences: What if we tried to simplify the design instead of adding more features?
What if we tried to finish this task today so we can relax on Sunday?
What if we tried to contact them via email instead of calling?
What if we tried to look at this problem from a different angle?
What if we tried to implement this suggestion during the next meeting?
native_notes: Uses the past tense (tried) to create a polite, hypothetical distance, making the suggestion sound less like a demand.

uzbek: Siz chindan ham ...ni o'ylab ko'rishingiz kerak
usage: Used when giving a strong, polite recommendation to someone to change their mind or take a specific action.
grammar_pattern: You really should consider + noun/V-ing
alternatives: I strongly suggest you look into...
example_sentences: You really should consider moving to a quieter area for your studies.
You really should consider this job offer, as it has better benefits.
If you want to improve, you really should consider taking a private class.
You really should consider the impact your decision might have on others.
You really should consider buying a laptop instead of a desktop.
native_notes: The word 'really' adds sincerity rather than just intensity. It makes the suggestion feel more personal.

expression: Don't you think it's time to...?
usage: A rhetorical way to nudge someone into doing something they have been putting off or avoiding.
grammar_pattern: Don't you think it's time to + V (base form)?
common_mistakes: Do you not think it is time for V-ing
Don't you think time is for...
alternatives: I think it's high time to...
example_sentences: Don't you think it's time to start preparing for your IELTS exam?
Don't you think it's time to update our software?
Don't you think it's time to tell them the truth?
Don't you think it's time to focus on your health?
Don't you think it's time to find a more efficient solution?
native_notes: Using 'Don't you think' makes the persuasion sound like an inquiry, which is less confrontational than a direct command.
russian: Вам не кажется, что пришло время...?

expression: It would be in your best interest to...
uzbek: Sizning manfaatlaringiz uchun ... qilsangiz yaxshi bo'lardi
usage: Used to persuade someone by highlighting the personal benefit or protection they will gain from doing something.
grammar_pattern: It would be in your best interest to + V (base form)
common_mistakes: It would be in your best interests of...
It would be on your best interest
example_sentences: It would be in your best interest to disclose all the facts before the meeting.
It would be in your best interest to accept the settlement offer.
It would be in your best interest to arrive early for the interview.
It would be in your best interest to take this training seriously.
It would be in your best interest to update your policy as soon as possible.
native_notes: This can sound very professional or, depending on the tone, slightly threatening (like a warning).
russian: Для твоего же блага было бы лучше, если бы ты это сделал.

usage: Used to give practical advice when you believe a specific choice will lead to a better outcome than the one the person is currently choosing.
grammar_pattern: You'd (You would) be better off + V-ing
common_mistakes: You'd be better off to do
alternatives: You'd have more luck if you...
example_sentences: You'd be better off studying in the library where it's quiet.
You'd be better off taking the train during rush hour.
You'd be better off getting a second opinion from another doctor.
You'd be better off applying for a different department.
You'd be better off focusing on your strengths instead of your weaknesses.
native_notes: Very common in everyday English. It is a soft way of saying 'your current plan is not very good'.

usage: Used to ask someone to pause and reconsider their negative position before making a final decision.
grammar_pattern: Just think about it + (tag question or exclamation)
alternatives: Try to see it from my point of view
example_sentences: We could finish the work much faster if we worked together; just think about it.
You could save so much money by cooking at home, just think about it.
If you don't take this offer now, you might regret it later—just think about it.
Traveling while you are young gives you so much experience; just think about it.
It's a huge opportunity for your career, just think about it before saying no.
native_notes: Often used as a final attempt to convince someone after presenting an argument.

uzbek: Bu oson tanlov (o'ylab o'tirishga ham hojat yo'q)
usage: Used to suggest that a decision is so obvious or beneficial that it requires very little thinking.
grammar_pattern: It's a no-brainer + to-infinitive / that clause
example_sentences: Choosing to study at that university was a no-brainer for me.
The salary offer was so high that accepting the job was a no-brainer.
Upgrading to the faster internet speed for only two dollars more is a no-brainer.
If you have the chance to travel abroad for free, it's a no-brainer.
Installing solar panels to save money on electricity is a complete no-brainer.
native_notes: Very common in spoken British English. Sounds natural and confident.
russian: Это простой выбор (вам даже не придется об этом думать)

usage: Used to steer a conversation towards your point of view and force the listener to acknowledge your logic.
grammar_pattern: Don't you agree that + clause?
example_sentences: Don't you agree that local businesses need more support from the government?
Don't you agree that social media has become a bit of a distraction lately?
Don't you agree that we should prioritize public transport over building more roads?
Don't you agree that quality is more important than quantity in fashion?
Don't you agree that children learn better when they are having fun?
native_notes: This is a rhetorical question that expects a 'yes'. It is highly persuasive.

usage: Used to point out a logical advantage when trying to convince someone to agree with your viewpoint.
grammar_pattern: Surely it makes sense to + verb
example_sentences: Surely it makes sense to finish the project today while we have the time.
Surely it makes sense to invest in new equipment to improve efficiency.
Surely it makes sense to book the tickets early to get a cheaper price.
Surely it makes sense to ask for professional advice in this situation.
Surely it makes sense to take a break when we are this tired.
native_notes: The word 'Surely' is a rhetorical device that implies the conclusion is obvious to any rational person.

uzbek: Agar biz ... qilsak nima bo'ladi / balki ... qilib ko'ramiz?
usage: Used in group discussions or negotiations to propose a hypothetical plan without sounding aggressive.
grammar_pattern: What if we were to + verb?
common_mistakes: What if we were to doing
example_sentences: What if we were to change our marketing strategy next month?
What if we were to invite more international experts to the conference?
What if we were to start the meeting an hour earlier to save time?
What if we were to postpone the decision until we have more data?
What if we were to reorganize the office layout for better collaboration?
native_notes: Using the past subjunctive 'were' makes the proposal sound polite, cautious, and professional.

expression: Just think of the benefits of
uzbek: Shunchaki ... ning foydasini bir o'ylab ko'ring
usage: Used to appeal to someone's emotions or logic by highlighting positive outcomes to encourage agreement.
grammar_pattern: Just think of the benefits of + noun/V-ing
alternatives: Imagine how much better it would be if
Think about what we could gain by
If we do this, we stand to gain
example_sentences: Just think of the benefits of exercising for thirty minutes a day.
Just think of the benefits of having a flexible working schedule.
Just think of the benefits of learning a second language for your career.
Just think of the benefits of buying local products for the environment.
Just think of the benefits of starting a savings account early.
native_notes: The 'Just' at the start acts as a soft invitation rather than an order, making it more persuasive.

expression: You really should give it a go
uzbek: Haqiqatan ham buni sinab ko'rishing kerak
usage: Used to encourage someone to try something they are hesitant about.
grammar_pattern: Subject + really + should + give it a go
common_mistakes: You really should give a go
You should give it to go
example_sentences: You really should give it a go; the new software is much faster.
I know you're nervous, but you really should give it a go.
It looks difficult, but you really should give it a go.
You really should give it a go before deciding you don't like it.
Even if you fail, you really should give it a go.
native_notes: 'Give it a go' is a very British idiomatic way of saying 'attempt something'. It sounds much more natural than 'try'.

usage: Used to persuade someone that an idea or option has significant value.
grammar_pattern: It is well worth + V-ing
common_mistakes: It is well worth to consider
example_sentences: It’s well worth considering the impact of climate change on our city.
The price is high, but it’s well worth considering the long-term benefits.
It’s well worth considering a different approach to this project.
I think it’s well worth considering his proposal before we vote.
It’s well worth considering the feedback from our customers.
native_notes: The word 'well' acts as an intensifier here. 'Worth' is always followed by the gerund (V-ing), never an infinitive (to V).

expression: You’d be far better off if you...
uzbek: Agar ... qilsang, senga ancha yaxshi bo'ladi
usage: Used to give advice that acts as a persuasive push towards a specific decision.
grammar_pattern: You'd be far better off + if + past simple
alternatives: It would be in your best interest to...
Your best bet would be to...
example_sentences: You’d be far better off if you learned to use professional software.
You’d be far better off if you invested in a good laptop.
You’d be far better off if you prepared for the exam a month in advance.
You’d be far better off if you listened to his advice.
You’d be far better off if you just told the truth from the start.
synonyms: It is in your interest to
native_notes: Adding 'far' makes the suggestion sound much more emphatic. It indicates that the current path is significantly less advantageous than the suggested one.
russian: Для тебя будет намного лучше, если ты это сделаешь

uzbek: Buning hech qanday zarari yo'q (qilib ko'rish kerak)
usage: Used to encourage someone to try something new or take a small risk.
grammar_pattern: There's no harm in + V-ing
common_mistakes: There is no harm to try
alternatives: Why not give it a try
example_sentences: There's no harm in checking the official website for more details.
There's no harm in asking for a discount if you're a regular customer.
There's no harm in trying a new learning method for a week.
There's no harm in applying for the job, even if you lack experience.
There's no harm in expressing your opinion during the meeting.
native_notes: Very common in everyday English to lower someone's anxiety about making a decision.
russian: В этом нет никакого вреда (надо попробовать)

usage: Used to convince someone that an effort or activity will produce good results.
grammar_pattern: It is + well + worth + your time
common_mistakes: It is worth of your time
It is worth to your time
alternatives: It's a great investment of time
example_sentences: I highly recommend this book; it's well worth your time.
Although the research is long, it's well worth your time.
Attending the conference is well worth your time if you want to network.
Learning a new language is well worth your time in the long run.
The museum exhibition is well worth your time.
native_notes: Using 'well' adds emphasis that the value is high.

expression: Think about it from this angle
uzbek: Bu masalaga shu tomondan qarab ko'ring
usage: Used to shift someone's perspective on a topic to reach an agreement.
grammar_pattern: Think about it + from this angle
alternatives: Consider it from a different perspective
example_sentences: Think about it from this angle: if we start now, we finish early.
I understand your concern, but think about it from this angle.
Think about it from this angle, and you might see why I disagree.
If you think about it from this angle, the solution seems obvious.
Don't be so quick to judge; think about it from this angle.
collocations: look at it from this angle
native_notes: Useful in academic discussions or debates to introduce a counter-point.
russian: Посмотрите на это под этим углом

usage: Used to suggest a new path or solution in a collaborative, non-confrontational way.
grammar_pattern: What if we + past tense verb (for hypothetical)
example_sentences: What if we tried a different route to avoid the traffic?
What if we tried focusing on one task at a time?
What if we tried to negotiate a better deal with the supplier?
What if we tried something completely different for our holiday this year?
What if we tried explaining our situation to the manager?
native_notes: Using the past tense ('tried') makes the suggestion sound softer and more hypothetical, which is standard in polite English.
